title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
hook: night one: seeds in a clay dish, a pot of water, and a festival that works like a course taken in order

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama came round to its last names: Shiva and Shakti as one, and Lalitambika, Lalita the mother. Did you end one thing the way it began? Tonight, the goddess's nine nights begin. Day one thousand one hundred nine.
screen: `THE LAST WORD IS MOTHER.` → `THE NINE NIGHTS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: In some homes in North India, the first night of Navaratri starts with dirt. A shallow clay dish, a layer of soil, a handful of barley seeds pressed in. A pot of water is set up beside it, or on it, with mango leaves and a coconut at its mouth, and a lamp is lit. Then, night by night, almost nothing seems to happen. And then something does. By the end of the festival, the dish is full of thin green shoots. Nine nights, and a lesson you can watch grow. Tonight, night one, and the idea that holds this whole stretch of the path together: Navaratri as a curriculum.
screen: `SOIL, SEEDS, A POT OF WATER.` → `NIGHT BY NIGHT.` → `A LESSON YOU CAN WATCH GROW.`

segments.voice: Navaratri means nine nights, and they belong to the goddess. There's more than one Navaratri in the year; the one this path keeps falls in autumn. And the Devi Mahatmya, the text the path read whole at the start of this year, points at that season itself. Near its end, the goddess speaks, and in paraphrase she says: at the great worship held in autumn, whoever hears this story of mine with devotion will be freed from troubles. So for some households the nights are also a reading plan, the Devi Mahatmya recited across them. Now, why call it a curriculum? Because the nights aren't nine copies of the same evening. They come in order, like a course. In some places each night has its own form of the goddess, its own color, its own offerings. Families who keep the festival don't all keep it the same way, and the regions differ a great deal: dancing in one place, a staircase of dolls in another, great images of Durga in another. But underneath, the shape repeats. You begin, you stay, and the staying does the work. One way of counting gives the first nights to Durga, the one who faces down whatever blocks the road. That makes night one the first day of school: you don't learn much yet, you just show up and plant something. That's what the dish of seeds is doing. Nobody expects shoots tonight. The seed is sown so that the coming nights have something to tend. The curriculum begins with a beginning, and trusts the rest to time.
screen: `NINE NIGHTS FOR THE GODDESS.` · `HEAR MY STORY IN AUTUMN.` · `IN ORDER, LIKE A COURSE.` · `NIGHT ONE: SHOW UP AND PLANT.` · then, large: `A BEGINNING, TRUSTED TO TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: planting. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one small thing you'd like to grow over the next nine nights. Not a resolution. A seed. A little more patience at dinner. Ten minutes of reading. Calling your grandmother. Hold it lightly, the way you'd hold a seed between two fingers. Then set it down in your mind, in good soil, and leave it there. No need to check on it yet. If you pray, you can offer it to the goddess on this first night, in your own words. If you don't, simply let it be planted. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Nine nights for the goddess, kept in order like a course. Night one: show up, and plant something. Today's word.
Your line: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Today, do the first small piece of the thing you planted, just once, and don't judge it yet. Day one thousand one hundred nine.

howItsDone: In some North Indian homes the first day of Navaratri begins with ghatasthapana: a water pot is installed for the goddess and barley is sown in soil to sprout through the nine nights; elsewhere the first night opens with dance, a display of dolls, or recitation of the Devi Mahatmya.

original.note: Sanskrit navarātri: nava, nine, and rātri, night.

trapdoor: what you thought: Navaratri is one long party.
what it means: nine nights for the goddess, kept in order, each with its own form and offering, like a course.
what a scholar hears: Devi Mahatmya 12, the goddess on the great autumn worship (śaratkāle mahāpūjā); sowing of barley with ghaṭasthāpana in parts of the north.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya 12 (the great worship in autumn; hearing the goddess's story)

notes: Devi Mahatmya 12 paraphrased: the goddess says that at the great annual worship in autumn, whoever hears this Mahatmya with devotion will be freed from troubles. Confirm verse (c. 12.11–12) and wording.

Ghatasthapana with barley (jau/jaware) sown and sprouting by the end: described as 'some homes in North India'; confirm the details (mango leaves, coconut, the dish placement) and that sprouting by the end is fair.
Spring (Chaitra) and autumn (Sharad) Navaratris are both kept; the script says only that there is more than one.
'In some places each night has its own form, color and offerings' — 'many' is general; confirm or soften.
1109 = night one, agreed with the 1112–1121 writer (who counts 1112 = night four). Only Durga's first stretch is introduced here; 1112 sets out the full three-by-three scheme.
